# The Weight of Small Things

I've been thinking about dust lately. Not in a poetic sense, though there's probably poetry in it somewhere. I mean actual dust—the particles that settle on picture frames and car dashboards, the stuff that accumulates in corners despite our best efforts to maintain order.

There's something honest about dust. It doesn't pretend. It just exists, evidence of time passing, of skin cells and textile fibers and whatever else we shed into the world. We fight it constantly, armed with cloths and sprays, but it always returns. It's not personal. It's just the nature of existing in physical space.

I mention this because I've realized I spend a lot of mental energy on things that don't matter. Not in the grand sense—I'm not having an existential crisis about the meaninglessness of existence. Rather, I'm noticing how much I worry about minor social interactions that anyone else has probably forgotten. A slightly awkward comment I made at a party three weeks ago. Whether someone took my joke the wrong way. If I sounded too eager or not eager enough in an email.

These thoughts are like dust. They settle in, accumulate, require constant attention to manage, and they'll just come back anyway.

The counterintuitive part is that recognizing this doesn't immediately fix it. You can't just intellectually understand that your anxiety is pointless and then stop being anxious. The brain doesn't work that way. It's more like understanding that a fear of falling is irrational while still feeling your stomach drop on a roller coaster. Knowledge and feeling are different currencies.

What does help, oddly enough, is lowering the bar for what constitutes a good day. I've been experimenting with this. A good day used to require: accomplishing major tasks, being productive, exercise, eating well, having an interesting thought, connecting meaningfully with someone, and not being anxious. That's a lot of requirements. That's a recipe for disappointment.

Now I'm testing: a good day is one where I didn't actively harm myself or others, where I did one thing that moved toward a goal, and where I noticed something interesting. The bar is on the floor. And somehow, I'm clearing it more often.

This probably sounds depressingly low-expectation. But there's freedom in it. When you're not aiming for perfection, when you're not trying to be exceptional every single day, something shifts. You start to notice small things without the pressure of them needing to be significant. A conversation that didn't go anywhere special becomes fine instead of a failure. A day of no accomplishments becomes neutral instead of wasted.

I think this is what people mean when they talk about acceptance, though that word has become so overused it's almost lost meaning. They don't mean giving up or becoming complacent. They mean releasing the grip on how things should be so you can actually experience how things are.

The problem with shoulding all over yourself—yes, I'm using "should" as a verb, grammatically dubious as that may be—is that you're never actually present. You're always comparing reality to the imagined standard. You're always in the gap between what is and what ought to be. That gap is exhausting to live in.

Here's what's strange: most of the people I admire don't seem to live in that gap. They seem to have somehow made peace with their own unremarkability. Not in a sad way. In a liberated way. They're free to be exactly whoever they are, not because they've achieved some enlightened state, but because they've stopped keeping score.

I wonder if that's the secret everyone pretends not to know. That the path to being interesting isn't trying harder to be interesting. It's being genuinely uninterested in the performance aspect. People sense that and respond to it. Authenticity is magnetic not because it's rare, but because it's so clearly effortless.

Of course, saying this and doing this are entirely different things. I still catch myself mid-concern about something trivial, still notice the anxiety rising. The difference is I now have this image of dust to work with. The thought will settle. I don't have to sweep it away immediately. I can let it sit there, acknowledge it, and move on with my day. Sometimes I'll still engage with the worry—that's fine too. But at least I'm not pretending it's actually important.

What I'm trying to get at, in this meandering way, is that I think we're all carrying around an impossible internal metric for what a day should look like, what a person should be, how conversations should go. And it's crushing us. Not visibly, usually. But in the quiet moments. In the 3 AM thoughts. In the way we brace ourselves for ordinary interactions.

What if we put that metric down? Not forever, not completely. Just sometimes. Just enough to breathe.

Just enough to notice that we're actually okay exactly as we are: imperfect, unremarkable, anxious sometimes, forgetting things, making awkward jokes, accumulating small failures and small victories in equal measure.

Just like everyone else.

The dust will still settle. Time will still pass. We'll still worry about things that don't matter. But maybe, if we're lucky, we'll also notice the sunlight coming through the window, illuminating those dust particles dancing in the air, and think: okay. This is what it looks like to be alive. This ordinary, dusty, imperfect thing. This is enough.
